abstract: To fully investigate the effects of heat treatment on proteins and lipids in sheep milk, lipidomics and Astral-DIA proteomics combined with parallel reaction monitoring methods were used to analyze the changes of lipids and proteins after heat treatment at 65 °C for 30 min and 95 °C for 15 s. A total of 79 and 381 differential lipids and proteins were identified respectively. Lipidomics results show that Triacylglycerol (16:1_17:1_16:2) was unique in raw milk, whereas diacylglycerol (20:1_22:1) was unique in 95 °C group. Choline metabolism in cancer was the core metabolic pathway linked with heat treatment. Additionally, the collagen alpha-3(VI) chain protein (COL6A3), folate receptor-like domain-containing protein (FOLR1), and serpin domain-containing protein (JEQ12_008015) gradually disappeared with increasing heating temperature. The differentially expressed proteins were mainly associated with metabolic pathways. These analysis provide scientific connotation for the production of high quality dairy products and the healthy development of the dairy industry.

Materials and methods
2.1
Reagents
All solvents and chemicals were of HPLC or LC-MS grade. Acetonitrile (ACN), methanol (MeOH), isopropanol (IPA), methyl tert-butyl ether (MTBE), and formic acid (FA) were obtained from Merck (Darmstadt, Germany). LC-MS grade water and acetonitrile were supplied by Thermo Scientific. Lipid standards were sourced from Avanti Polar Lipids (Alabaster, AL, USA). Sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS, China National Pharmaceutical), mass spectrometry-grade trypsin (Promega, V5280) and acetone (Beijing Chemical Factory) were used. Ultrapure water was generated using a Milli-Q system (Millipore, Bedford, MA, USA).
2.2
Sample collection
Sheep milk was collected at the Yuansheng Ranch in Jinchang City (Gansu Province, China). The selected sheep are all healthy and disease-free, and in good growth condition. Approximately 15–30, 45–60, 100–120 and 160–180 days after the birth of the lambs, 60 samples were collected at each stage. Ten samples were randomly selected from each of the four lactation groups and mixed to form one biological replicate. These samples were then heated at 65 °C for 30 min and at 95 °C for 15 s. Samples were presrved at −80 °C.
2.3
Lipid and protein extraction
For lipid extraction, each sample was defrosted on ice, vortexed for 10 s, and 20 μL was mixed with extraction solvent (MTBE: MeOH =3:1,
v
/v) containing internal standard mixture of 1 mL. Subsequent to stirring the entire mixture for 15 min, ultrapure water of 0.2 mL was administered. At 4 °C, centrifuge at 12,000 r/min for 1 min. Transfer 200 μL of the supernatant to the corresponding numbered 1.5 mL centrifuge tube and concentrate at 20 °C until completely dry. The dried extraction was diluted with 0.2 mL complex solution (acetone/isopropanol, 1:1 v/v) preceding to LC- MS/MS analysis.
To efficiently extract the protein and keep it dissolved and stable, SDT cracking solution (4 % sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS), 100 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.6) was added to each sample. Samples were then transferred to eppendorf (EP) tubes, boiled in a water bath, subjected to ultrasonic crushing for 2 min. The supernatant was taken for quantitative analysis by bicinchoninic acid (BCA) Protein Assay Kit (BeyoTime, China). After quality detection and enzymatic hydrolysis, the proteins were subjected to LC-MS/MS analysis. After quality detection and enzymatic hydrolysis, the proteins were subjected to LC – MS/MS analysis.
2.4
Lipid LC–MS/MS analysis
The extracted sample were examined using an a LC–electrospray ionization (ESI)-MS/MS system. The ESI-triple quadrupole linear ion trap-MS (QTRAP)-MS was coupled to the effluent on an alternate basis (SCIEX, Framingham, MA, USA). ESI source running parameters are as follows: source temperature 500 °C, ion source, turbo spray; ion spray voltage (IS), −4500 V (negative) and 5500 V (positive); ion source curtain gas (CUR); the medium was CAD or collision gas. For Triple quadrupole (QQQ) scans results Multiple Reaction Monitoring (MRM) tests were used and the collision gas (nitrogen) were adjusted at 5 psi. Based on the metabolites that flushed throughout each phase, a particular set of MRM transitions was tracked. Each extract was analyzed once. All the samples were mixed in equal volumes to prepare quality control (QC) samples, and a QC sample was inserted after each analysis of 6 experimental samples. The lipid qualitative analysis is based on retention time (RT) and the information of parent and daughter ion pairs. The quantitative analysis adopts the MRM of triple quadrupole mass spectrometry. By selectively screening parent ions and characteristic fragment ions, the specificity and repeatability of detection are significantly improved. All lipid chromatographic peaks are integrated, and peak area correction across samples is performed. The lipid identification is all verified by commercial standards, and used for retention time correction and fragment ion confirmation.
2.5
UHPLC-astral LC/MS DIA
The mobile phases A (formic acid (0.1 %) and water (100 %)), and B (formic acid (0.1 %) and acetonitrile (80 %)) were prepared. A orbitrap astral mass spectrometer mass spectrometer was used (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA), the ion spray voltage was set to 1.9 kV, the temperature of ion transfer tube was adjusted to 290 °C, and the mass spectrum was acquired in a data dependent acquisition mode, with a full first-stage mass spectrometry scanning range of 380–980
m
/
z
. The primary MS resolution was set to 240,000 (200 m/z); the number of DIA windows was 300; the secondary m/z acquisition range was from 150 to 2000; the sub-ion resolution astral was set to 80,000; and the maximum injection time was 3 ms. The peptide sample was separated and analyzed by the UHPLC-Astral system. The mass spectrometry detection adopted the data-independent acquisition (DIA) mode. Protein identification was carried out by comparing the DIA data with the Uniprotkb-
Ovis aries
(sheep) [9940] database, and processed using the DIA-NN software (version 1.8.1). All identification results were strictly controlled at a false discovery rate (FDR) of 1 %. Protein quantification was based on the chromatographic peak area of the extracted parent ions.
2.6
LC-PRM/MS
Two micrograms of each sample was taken for LC-PRM/MS analysis. Chromatographic separation was performed using the nanoliter flow rate Easy nLC 1200 chromatography system (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). The buffer was prepared as follows: Liquid A was 0.1 % formic acid aqueous solution, liquid B was 0.1 % formic acid, acetonitrile and water mixed solution (with 95 % acetonitrile). The peptides were isolated and then subjected to targeted PRM mass spectrometry using a QExactive HF-X mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). Secondary mass spectrometry of peptides was performed according to the following methods: Following each complete MS scan, the precursor
m
/
z
of the target peptide segment is sequentially chosen based on the inclusion list for the secondary mass spectrometry scan analysis (MS2), with MS2 resolution set to 30,000@m/z200. Additional parameters applied include: AGC target of 1e6, maximum IT of 100 ms, MS2 activation type of HCD, isolation window of 1.6Th, and normalized collision energy of 28. For each sample, three technical replicates were conducted for the on-machine testing. The average value was taken to ensure the accuracy of the quantification. The resulting RAW mass spectrometry file was processed using the software Skyline 4.1 on the PRM data.
2.7
Bioinformatics analysis
Principal component analysis (PCA) was conducted using the prcomp function in R (
www.r-project.org
), following the normalization of the data to unit variance for unsupervised computing. The outcomes of hierarchical cluster analysis for both metabolites and samples were displayed as heatmaps accompanied by dendrograms. Additionally, Pearson correlation coefficients (PCC) between samples were computed using the cor function in R and visualized as heatmaps. GO functional analysis was conducted against a non-redundant protein database using the InterProscan program. Identified metabolites were annotated using the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) COMPOUND Database (
http://www.kegg.jp/kegg/compound/
) and annotated metabolites were mapped to the KEGG PATHWAY Database (
http://www.kegg.jp/kegg/pathway.html
).
2.8
Statistical analysis
For the two-group analysis, differential metabolites were identified based on a
P
-value less than 0.05 and a variable importance in projection (VIP) score greater than 1, determined using Student's
t
-test. For multi-group analysis, differential metabolites were recognized using VIP > 1 and
P
< 0.05 (ANOVA). Proteins that showed significant differential expression were those displaying a P < 0.05, FC ≥ 1.5 or ≤ 1/1.5.

Introduction
Milk serve as a significant source of nutrition for humans and can provide the proteins, lipids, and other energy required for human development (
Collard & McCormick, 2021
). Sheep milk is a small-breed milk, often referred to as the “the king of milk,” which has higher nutritional value, dry matter, protein, and fat content, than that from goats or cows, and is closer to human breast milk and has better effects on the human body (
Caboni et al., 2019
). Sheep milk has many beneficial effects, including antitumor, antioxidant, antibacterial, and hypoglycemic properties (
Flis & Molik, 2021
). Other studies have found that sheep milk and its products can effectively prevent diabetes and cancer and can be used to improve intestinal health (
Fatahi et al., 2021
;
Hsu et al., 2018
;
Zhang et al., 2024
). The dairy sheep industry has been steadily developing, and has great potential for further development (
Pulina et al., 2018
). With the improvement in power consumption and increasing demand for sheep milk, it has become a new research hotspot in the development of functional dairy ingredients.
Heat treatment is the most common processing method for industrial milk treatment and this is also a significant approach for inhibiting bacterial growth and killing pathogenic microorganisms in raw milk (
Dumpler et al., 2020
). However, the heat treatment temperature if too high will destroy some nutrients, leading to protein denaturation, loss of important active proteins, and changes in milk characteristics (
Lu et al., 2023
). The principle of pasteurization is to heat raw milk at a lower temperature and kill most pathogens and spoilage bacteria. This can maintain the taste and nutrients of milk to a maximum extent but does not completely kill the pathogens and spoilage bacteria (
Li et al., 2020
). All of these processes change the thermal stability of milk. Some scholars have carried out different heat treatments of milk to study the changes in milk composition and function (
Bai et al., 2023
). Studied the influence of ultra-high-temperature processes on the changes in metabolites in milk and found that these processing methods affect the content of some components in milk. In terms of proteins, examine the impact of heat treatment on the individual milk proteins α-casein, β-casein, and β-lactoglobulin by sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE). The production of the whey protein–casein polymer complex escalated markedly with elevated heat treatment duration and temperature (
Čurlej et al., 2022
). Studied the effect of various heat treatment of goat milk on the size, rheology, and texture of micelles of acidic gels and casein in set yogurt (
Hovjecki et al., 2020
). However, there are no comprehensive studies on the impact of different heat treatments on lipids and proteins in sheep milk. The effects of different heat treatment methods on the nutritional changes in milk from cows, goats, and camels has been reported previously (
Fatih et al., 2021
;
Qian et al., 2017
). Heat-treated camel milk at low temperature (65 °C) or high temperature (100 °C) and found that the corresponding degradation of lactose, cysteine and methionine at high temperature affected the changes in the functional characteristics of intestinal flora (
Shao & Wang, 2018
). In addition, some studies on the consequences of heat treatment on milk lipids and proteins have shown that heating breast milk can affect the concentration of immunomodulatory proteins, especially secretory immunoglobulin A, lysozyme, and lactoferrin (
Chang et al., 2013
).
Although heat treatment-related proteins and lipids have been reported, most of them are cow and goat milk studies (
Zhang et al., 2022
). However, there are significant differences in the nutritional components of sheep milk (such as high protein content, high fat content, small fat globule diameters, etc.), and its heat sensitivity may cause unique nutritional losses and functional deterioration. These differences make it difficult for the existing research conclusions on cow and goat milk to directly guide the processing practices of sheep milk. In addition, the effect of heat treatment on only one component (lipid) has been reported (
Pan et al., 2024
). The synergistic changes in protein-lipid interactions during the heat treatment process have not yet been systematically revealed. As the core nutritional components, the comprehensive stability of these two factors directly determines the product quality and bioavailability. Therefore, in order to fill the research gap in the multi-component cooperative response mechanism of sheep milk during thermal processing, lipidomics and Astral-data-independent acquisition (DIA) proteomics were used to research the impact of various heat treatments on the protien and lipid contents of sheep milk. Heat-related proteins and small molecules were screened, and their functions were predicted by Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) annotation analysis. In addition, the identified proteins associated with heat treatment were validated by parallel reaction monitoring (PRM). The research results will provide precise parameters for optimizing the thermal processing technology of sheep milk, maximizing the retention of its high-value nutritional properties, promoting the transformation of the sheep milk industry from “mass production” to “high quality”, and meeting consumers' health needs for high-nutrition dairy products.

3
Results
3.1
Lipid composition of different heat treatment groups
A total of 978 lipids were identified by LC-MS/MS. The positive and negative ion mode lipid metabolites of quality control (QC) samples were detected, which showed that there were more ion peaks, the main samples had high peak response intensity, and the separation effect was good. Moreover, the curve overlap in the total ion flow diagram of positive and negative modes of QC samples is high, indicating that the retention time and peak intensity are consistent, indicating that the signal is relatively stable when the same sample is tested at different times (Supplementary material Fig. S1-S4).
Fig. 1
A shows the Venn diagram of lipids identified in the raw milk (SM, not heat-treated, stored at −80 °C), 65 °C and 95 °C groups. A total of 971, 972, and 969 lipids were identified in the three groups, respectively, and one lipid was unique in the raw milk, which was triacylglycerol (TG;16:1_17:1_16:2). In the 65 °C group, there were two unique lipids, lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC; 0:0/20:0) and ceramide (Cer; d17:1/24:1), and in the 95 °C group, there was one unique lipid, diacylglycerol (DG; 20:1_22:1). Each of the three groups contained 960 lipids.

B–D shows the types and contents of lipids identified in the three milk groups. The most important lipid was TG, which accounted for more than 30 %, followed by phosphatidylethanolamine (PE), phosphatidylcholine (PC), and DG, which accounted for more than 5 %. In general, there was little difference in the overall lipid content among the groups after heat treatment.

Venn diagram (A) of lipids identified by different heat treatments. Pie charts of lipid proportions in the raw milk (SM) (B), 65 °C (C), and 95 °C (D) groups.

3.2
Differential lipids analysis of different heat treatments
We then performed PCA (
Fig. 2
A) and found significant differences between the groups. The proportion of variance explained by the first principal coordinate (PC1) to the differentiated samples was 50.73 %, and the contribution percentage of the second principal coordinate (PC2) to the differentiated samples was 9.99 %. The contribution percentage of the third principal coordinate (PC3) to the differentiation of the samples was 7.25 %. The orthogonal partial least-squares discriminant analysis (OPLS-DA) model was additionally employed to visualize the separation in the different heat-treated samples (
Fig. 2
B), which showed a significant differences between the three sample types. Using statistical analysis, the lipid types with significant differences (VIP > 1,
P
< 0.05) in the milk of the different groups were screened.
Fig. 2
C shows the heat map of the differential lipid cluster analysis, and
Fig. 2
D–F show the volcanic maps of the differential lipids. The abundance of Cer (t21:2/18:1), TG (16:1_17:1_16:2), and phosphatidylserine (PS; 12:0_15:1) was relatively high, but the differences were large among the three groups. They were significantly down-regulated in groups 65 °C and 95 °C, due to changes caused by heating. In the 95 °C vs. SM group, 13 lipids were up-regulated, and 19 lipids were down-regulated; in the 95 °C vs. 65 °C group, nine lipids were up-regulated and 12 lipids were down-regulated; and in the 65 °C vs. SM group, there were 14 up-regulated and 12 down-regulated lipids. The detailed data can be found in the supplementary material Table S1.

Principal component analysis (PCA) (A), orthogonal partial least-squares discriminant analysis (B), heat map (C), and volcano plot lipid results for the 95 °C vs. SM (D), 95 °C vs. 65 °C (E), and 65 °C vs. SM (F) groups.

3.3
KEGG pathway analysis of differential lipids
To predict the function of these lipids, the lipid that were differentially were subjected to KEGG pathway enrichment analysis. The first 20 significantly enriched pathways are shown in
Fig. 3
. In the 95 °C vs. SM group, the main element involved probably differential lipids in Leishmaniasis, glycine, serine, and threonine metabolism. In the 95 °C vs. 65 °C groups, the differential lipids were mainly involved in glycerophospholipid and choline metabolism in cancer. In the 65 °C vs SM group, the differential lipids were primarily involved in choline and sphingolipid metabolism in cancer. These differential lipids are primarily involved in various metabolic processes and play as an important roles in immunity and cancer.
Fig. 3
Results of the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway enrichment analysis of differential lipids.

3.4
Protein composition under different heating treatments
DIA proteomic technology was used to identify and analyze proteins from the different heating groups (Supplementary material Table S2-S3). As shown in the Venn diagram (
Fig. 4
A), 1870, 1800, and 1909 proteins were identified in the SM, 65 °C and 95 °C groups, respectively, indicating that the heat treatment did not cause a substantial loss in the number of protein types; however, the numbers of specific proteins did change considerably (SM: 17 types, 65 °C: 14 types, 95 °C: 86 types). Of note, the number of proteins common to all three treatment groups was as high as 1690, constituting the core part of the milk protein group. Principal component analysis (PCA) (
Fig. 4
B) further revealed the distribution characteristics among the three groups of samples: PC1 and PC2, with explanation rates of 30.01 % and 19.99 %, respectively, jointly explained approximately 50 % of the intergroup variation. Although the repeated samples within each group showed good clustering (indicating good repeatability), the positions of the different heat treatment groups in the PCA space showed a significant separation trend, particularly in the PC1 direction. This result clearly indicates that while the core protein group remains relatively stable, different heat treatment intensities (particularly the 95 °C high-temperature treatment) can considerably change the overall composition and structure of the milk protein group, resulting in detectable deviations in its molecular characteristics. This deviation may be caused by various factors, including protein thermal denaturation, aggregation/precipitation, modification due to the Maillard reaction, and changes in solubility/extraction efficiency, etc.
Fig. 4
Venn diagram (A), PCA (B), heat map (C), and volcano plot of the protein results for 95C vs. SM (D), 95C vs. 65C (E) and 65C vs. SM (F).
Fig. 4
Based on strict statistical criteria (
P
< 0.05 and FC ≥ 1.5 or ≤ 1/1.5), we identified a total of 381 differentially expressed proteins (DEPs), highlighting the extensive impact of heat treatment on protein abundance. The hierarchical clustering analysis of the TOP 50 DEPs (
Fig. 4
C) clearly divides them into three protein clusters with different expression patterns, suggesting that proteins of different categories have distinct response mechanisms to heat treatment. The volcano plot (
Fig. 4
D-F) visually presented the distribution of DEPs among the groups. The analysis revealed that the collagen alpha-3 (VI) chain protein (COL6A3), folate receptor-like domain-containing protein (FOLR1), and serpin domain-containing protein (JEQ12_008015) were most abundant in the SM group, and showed a significant dose-dependent decrease as the heating temperature increased from 65 °C to 95 °C. The reduction of these proteins may be directly related to their thermal instability. For example, COL6A3, as a structural protein, may be susceptible to heat-induced conformational changes or degradation; the decrease of FOLR1 may suggest that heat processing may negatively impact the bioavailability of folate in milk. Notably, an uncharacterized protein (A0A6P3E869) had a lower abundance in the SM group and the 65 °C group, but its relative content significantly increased after heating at 95 °C. This phenomenon is particularly interesting, as it suggests that this protein may have unique thermal stability. Alternatively, through conformational changes, it may expose new epitopes, thereby enhancing detectability during high-temperature processing or even originate from heat-induced peptides or modified products. Functional analysis of this protein will be a key entry point for understanding the specific effects of high-temperature processing on the functional properties of milk proteins. These specific response DEPs provide important targets for in-depth research on the specific molecular mechanisms of heat treatment affecting the functions of milk proteins.
3.5
GO enrichment and KEGG pathway analysis of differentially expressed proteins
To better understand the potential biological significance of the 381 DEPs, we conducted a systematic pathway enrichment analysis usng Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG). GO enrichment analysis (
Fig. 5
A) revealed that, at the biological process (BP) level, the DEPs were significantly enriched for the “cofactor metabolic process term,” which plays a dominant role both in upregulating and downregulating DEPs. This indicates that thermal treatment profoundly affects the homeostasis of protein-related factors, including vitamins and minerals in sheep milk, which may directly relate to its nutritional value (e.g., vitamin retention rate) and enzymatic activity. At the cellular component (CC) level, “cytoskeleton” was the most significantly enriched item, and it also performed prominently in both the upregulation and downregulation of the DEPs. This strongly suggests that proteins related to the cytoskeleton are highly sensitive to heat stress; disruption or reorganization of their structural integrity may be an important molecular basis for the changes in the physicochemical properties of sheep milk proteins (such as viscosity, colloid stability). At the molecular function (MF) level, “organic cyclic compound binding and heterocyclic compound binding” were the most core functional categories. These functions are usually related to the binding of molecules such as nucleotides, coenzymes, and heme, and their enrichment further supports the notion that thermal treatment extensively disturbed the protein network related to cofactor metabolism and enzyme function. In summary, the GO analysis clearly delineates the core functional roles of the DEPs: first, that they are widely involved in various metabolic processes and play key roles in maintaining cytoskeletal structure and mediating (hetero) cyclic compound binding to regulate biological activity; and second, that these functional changes collectively constitute the molecular network by which thermal treatment affects the biological characteristics of sheep milk.
Fig. 5
Gene Ontology enrichment (A) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes pathway enrichment analysis (B) of differential protein.
Fig. 5
Furthermore, analysis of the top 20 significantly enriched DEP pathways revealed (
Fig. 5
B) that metabolic-related pathways were dominant. Among them, pathways such as “seleno-compound metabolism,” “aldosterone-regulated sodium reabsorption,” and “drug metabolism via cytochrome P450” were particularly significant. The enrichment of the “seleno-compound metabolism” pathway suggested that heat treatment may affect the abundance or activity of selenium proteins like glutathione peroxidase, thereby potentially influencing the antioxidant capacity of sheep milk. The enrichment of the “drug metabolism via cytochrome P450 pathway” term, although seemingly unexpected, may reflect the heat sensitivity of proteins with similar metabolic enzyme activity (or pollutant-binding proteins) present in sheep milk, which is worthy of further exploration for its association with the potential bioactive substances or elimination of foreign compounds in sheep milk. Enrichment of the “aldosterone-regulated sodium reabsorption” pathway might point to the impact of heat treatment on ion transport proteins, such as sodium channels or sodium‑potassium pump-related subunits, which could be related to heat treatment-mediated alterations in the functional properties of whey proteins, such as water-holding capacity. Not only did these pathway analysis results reveal the specific biological processes involved with the DEPs, they more importantly provided a new perspective and molecular-level explanatory framework for understanding how heat treatment reshapes the physiological and biochemical characteristics of sheep milk by interfering with key metabolic and regulatory pathways.
3.6

4
Discussion
In this study, sheep milk was heated at low temperature (65 °C for 30 min) and high temperature (95 °C for 15 s). In the SM, 65 °C and 95 °C groups, 971, 972 and 969 lipids and 1870, 1800 and 1909 proteins were identified respectively. A total of 79 and 381 differential lipids and proteins were identified respectively.
The lipid with the greatest differences among different groups was screened for analysis because it might be related to heat treatment. TG (16:1_17:1_16:2) was unique in the raw sheep milk (SM) group. It might be due to the high temperature that Triacylglycerol (TG) was degraded or converted into glycerol and fatty acids (
Cerk et al., 2018
). This result is consistent with the existing research reports (
Korte et al., 2023
). TG turnover is associated with daytime heat-induced stomatal opening, and effective stomatal opening during heat stress requires high acylglycerol turnover. In addition, DG (20:1_22:1) was unique in 95 °C group. Diacylglycerol (DG) is a structural lipid in TG, in which one fatty acid is replaced by a hydroxyl group. In the last several years, dietary DG has been shown to reduce blood lipid, and reduce visceral fat and inhibit weight gain (
Cooke & Kazanietz, 2022
). Although there are currently no research reports on the direct correlation between DG and heat treatment, since DG is closely related to TG and TG is known to have a significant correlation with the heat treatment process, it can be reasonably inferred that DG is also closely related to the heat treatment process. However, TG (16:1_17:1_16:2), DG (20:1_22:1), Cer (t21:2/18:1) and PS (12:0_15:1) are rarely reported. To predict the function of these lipids, we performed KEGG pathway enrichment analysis for differential lipids (
Fig. 3
) and found that these differential lipids are engaged in a variety of metabolic processes and play significant roles in immunity and cancer (Wu et al., 2023). This suggests that there are specific functional components in sheep milk that may have preventive or therapeutic effects on diseases, and further exploration is needed.
Beyond lipid composition, we also investigated the effects of heating on the proteins in sheep milk using Astral-DIA proteomics, which has the advantages of good reproducibility and high quantitative accuracy. The analysis found that the relative content of the collagen alpha-3(VI) chain protein (COL6A3), folate receptor-like domain-containing protein (FOLR1), and serpin domain-containing protein (JEQ12_008015) were the most abundant proteins in raw milk but these gradually disappeared with increasing heating temperature. Therefore, we speculate that these three proteins will be greatly damaged in spatial structure or undergo degradation due to the influence of high temperature. Subsequently, targeted verification was carried out through PRM. The fold change between the 95 °C group and SM group were 0.42, 0.68, and 0.81 respectively (
Table 1
), which were consistent with the results of DIA proteome sequencing. As we expected, there have been relevant research reports on the relationship between serpin domain-containing protein and heat treatment. Serine domain-containing proteins exist widely in organisms, play a role in digestion, and participate in pathogen clearance, extracellular matrix remodeling and cell migration (
Qin et al., 2022
). Some studies have shown that heating treatment may destroy the structure of its active center, leading to denaturation and loss of activity (
Chao et al., 2020
). Although no research has pointed out the relationship between folate receptor-like domain-containing protein, serpin domain-containing protein and heat treatment yet, they play an extremely important role. The collagen alpha-3 (VI) chain, encoded by the gene
COL6A3
, is one of the three subunits of collagen VI, a microfibrous component of the extracellular matrix that is essential for the stable assembly process of collagen VI and is also important in cancer progression (
Wang & Pan, 2020
). Folic acid is a B vitamin that plays a role in one‑carbon metabolism, and folic acid receptors are one of the three main types of folic acid transporters, with folic acid receptors
FOLR1
and
FOLR2
being overexpressed in a variety of cancers (
Holm & Hansen, 2020
;
Nawaz & Kipreos, 2022
). To predict the function of the DEPs, GO and KEGG enrichment analyses were performed on selected DEPs (
Fig. 5
). They play a major role in the cytoskeleton and compound synthesis, and regulate many pathways, such as selenium metabolism and aldosterone regulation of sodium. This suggests that heating can affect the stability of active proteins in sheep milk, thereby influencing the value and efficacy of sheep milk itself.
In summary, this study identified lipids and proteins related to the heat treatment of sheep milk and predicted their respective functions. However, this study also has certain limitations. It has not yet conducted research on different breeds of sheep. Besides, the functions of these lipids and proteins have not been fully studied. The next step is to further verify and explore the functions of these unique lipids and proteins and their relationship with heat treatment, and by setting different gradients of temperature and time to process sheep milk, to find the most suitable processing conditions, thereby improving the processing technology of dairy products. Our findings enhance the understanding of sheep milk while providing a direction for the development of high-quality milk products to support the efficient and rapid development of the dairy industry.
5
Conclusions
In summary, 971, 972 and 969 lipids were detected in sheep milk treated at 65 °C for 30 min and 95 °C for 15 s, respectively. TG (16:1:17:1_16:2) was unique in the SM group, while DG (20:1:22:1) was unique in the 95 °C group. In addition, we used DIA proteomic methods to detect 1870, 1800, and 1909 proteins in the SM, 65 °C, and 95 °C groups, respectively, and GO and KEGG enrichment analyses further explored the significant differences in metabolic pathway activity among the different heat-treated samples. These results contribute to the understanding of the effects of different heat treatments on the lipids and proteins in sheep milk, providing insights into the potential development of targeted functional sheep milk products and contributing to the healthy development of the dairy sheep sector.
